name: Dark Perilla Purple
lede: Dark Perilla Purple darkens [[perilla-purple]], named for the red-leaved perilla herb, and Albrecht Dürer's paintings carry it at nearly thirteen times our archive's average rate.

sections.title: A darkened herb color
sections.body:
The name pairs dark with [[perilla-purple]], named for *Perilla*, a mint-family herb grown for its deep red-purple leaves and used in East Asian cooking, medicine and dye [1]. Ridgway charted this darker tone in *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* (1912), plate XXXVII, hue 65′′, tone m, and the ISCC-NBS *Dictionary of Color Names* carried it forward in 1955 as block 259 [1].

Its nearest measured neighbor is [[purple-brown]], 2.7 units off and almost the same color; [[dark-maroon-purple]] and [[hay-s-maroon]] sit close behind, both a little redder, and [[umber-brown]] a touch further still at 4.2 units [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A match for this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 158 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.7 per cent, as photographed [3]. It is strongest in Albrecht Dürer's work, 4 of his 47 paintings, nearly 12.8 times the archive's overall rate, and in Henri Matisse's, 3 of 50, about nine times the rate [3]. The earliest dated match is a Roman-period portrait from around the year 100, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].
